plan: SAT R&W batch 67: 8 new items on new passages CLD-P-SAT-RW-000600..000607 (Andrews Gobi expeditions WIC, Oviraptor cross-text, bird-feeder quantitative evidence, Ida B. Wells purpose, Octavia Butler finite verb, Paul Laurence Dunbar possessive, Machu Picchu transition, Mary Anning synthesis). Topics checked against every bank and the combined bank. Plus S066-03 and S066-04 resubmitted as revision 2 on their previously unbanked passages. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Cars and camels
passages.text: In the 1920s, the naturalist Roy Chapman Andrews led a series of expeditions into Mongolia's Gobi Desert that were unusually ______: the teams traveled in automobiles, which were supplied with gasoline and food by caravans of more than one hundred camels sent ahead of them.

passages.title: An egg thief?
passages.text:
Text 1
In 1924, paleontologist Henry Fairfield Osborn named a newly found dinosaur Oviraptor, meaning "egg seizer," because its skeleton lay on top of a nest of eggs that were thought to belong to another dinosaur, Protoceratops. Osborn concluded that the animal had died while raiding the nest.

Text 2
In the 1990s, researchers working in the same region found an embryo of an oviraptor-like dinosaur inside an egg of the same type. They later found oviraptorid skeletons crouched over nests with their arms spread around the eggs, in a posture much like that of brooding birds.

passages.title: Feeder visits
passages.text:
A student counted the birds that visited a feeder in the hour after sunrise on four mornings. On two mornings the feeder held sunflower seed, and on two it held millet.
Sunflower: 34 visits and 30 visits
Millet: 12 visits and 16 visits
The student claims that the birds strongly preferred sunflower seed to millet.

passages.title: Counting the evidence
passages.text: In 1892, after three of her friends were murdered by a mob in Memphis, the journalist Ida B. Wells began investigating lynchings across the American South. Many white newspapers claimed that the victims had committed serious crimes. Using newspaper reports, court records, and interviews, Wells showed that in case after case the accusations were unproven or false, and she published her findings in the pamphlet Southern Horrors that year.

passages.title: A first for the genre
passages.text: Octavia E. Butler, whose novels include Kindred and Parable of the Sower, ______ the first science fiction writer to receive a MacArthur Fellowship, an award often called a "genius grant," in 1995.

passages.title: Poems for passengers
passages.text: After high school, Paul Laurence Dunbar, the son of formerly enslaved parents, worked as an elevator operator in Dayton, Ohio. He wrote poems between trips and in 1893 paid to have his first collection, Oak and Ivy, printed. The ______ passengers became some of his first readers, buying copies for a dollar each.

passages.title: Never lost
passages.text: Machu Picchu, a stone city high in the Andes of Peru, was built in the mid-1400s for the Inca ruler Pachacuti and was abandoned around the time of the Spanish conquest a century later. ______ it was never entirely forgotten: when the American explorer Hiram Bingham arrived in 1911, local farmers were living on its terraces, and a farmer guided him there.

passages.title: Notes on a fossil hunter
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Mary Anning (1799–1847) collected fossils on the cliffs near Lyme Regis, England.
- She found the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaur, a marine reptile, in 1823.
- As a woman, she could not join the Geological Society of London.
- Scientists often bought her fossils and described them in publications without naming her.
- Today she is recognized as an important early paleontologist.

passages.title: Soaking seeds
passages.text:
A student soaked bean seeds in water for different lengths of time before planting and recorded the percent that germinated.
No soaking: 40%
6 hours: 62%
12 hours: 78%
24 hours: 77%
The student claims that soaking longer than 12 hours provided no additional benefit.

passages.title: Lines in the desert
passages.text:
Text 1
In the mid-twentieth century, the German mathematician Maria Reiche spent decades studying the Nazca lines, huge figures and long straight lines scratched into the desert of southern Peru. She argued that many of the lines pointed to the rising and setting positions of the Sun and stars and served as an astronomical calendar.

Text 2
In 1968, the astronomer Gerald Hawkins tested this idea by comparing the directions of many lines with the positions of astronomical events. He found that the lines matched such events no more often than lines pointing in random directions would. Later researchers have proposed that the lines were paths walked in rituals, some possibly connected to water.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: caravans of more than one hundred camels sent ahead of them
candidates.explanation: Expeditions combining automobiles with large camel supply caravans were complex and carefully organized, or "elaborate."

A.rationale: Nothing suggests the expeditions were hidden.

B.rationale: Sending supply caravans ahead suggests careful planning, not haste.

C.rationale: Automobiles plus a caravan of more than a hundred camels is the opposite of modest.

hints: What does the explanation after the colon describe?
candidates.remember: Let the explanation after the colon define the blank.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to Osborn's conclusion in Text 1?

choices.A: They would agree that oviraptorids raided nests but say they ate only Protoceratops eggs.
choices.B: They would argue that the animal was probably guarding its own eggs, not stealing others.
choices.C: They would argue that Protoceratops was the animal that died on top of the nest.
choices.D: They would claim that dinosaurs were unlikely to have built nests at all.

candidates.evidence: crouched over nests with their arms spread around the eggs
candidates.explanation: The embryo shows the eggs were oviraptorid eggs, and the brooding posture suggests the animal was protecting its own nest, not raiding another's.

A.rationale: Text 2's findings show the eggs belonged to oviraptorids, not Protoceratops.

C.rationale: The skeleton on the nest was identified as Oviraptor in both texts.

D.rationale: Text 2 describes dinosaurs crouched over nests.

hints: Whose eggs were they, according to Text 2?

strategy.explanation: Compare Osborn's assumption with the later evidence.

candidates.remember: New evidence can reverse an earlier interpretation.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the student's claim?

choices.A: Both sunflower mornings had about twice as many visits as either millet morning.
choices.B: The feeder received 34 visits on the first sunflower morning, its highest total.
choices.C: Visits on the two millet mornings differed by 4.
choices.D: The feeder received 92 visits in all across the four mornings.

candidates.evidence: the birds strongly preferred sunflower seed to millet
candidates.explanation: Each sunflower morning (34, 30) had roughly twice as many visits as either millet morning (12, 16), which supports a strong preference.

B.rationale: A single morning cannot show a preference.

C.rationale: This compares millet mornings with each other, not the two seeds.

D.rationale: A total does not compare the two seeds.

hints: What comparison does the claim require?

strategy.explanation: Compare the two kinds of seed directly.

candidates.remember: Support a comparison with data from both groups.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To explain how Memphis newspapers were printed and distributed in the 1890s
choices.B: To argue that court records were the most reliable source available to Wells
choices.C: To describe how a journalist used evidence to challenge a widely repeated claim
choices.D: To compare Wells's reporting with that of other journalists of her time

candidates.evidence: Wells showed that in case after case the accusations were unproven or false
candidates.explanation: The text describes what prompted Wells's investigation, the claim she challenged, and the evidence she used to show it was false.

A.rationale: The text does not describe printing or distribution.

B.rationale: The text lists court records as one of several sources.

D.rationale: The text does not compare Wells with other journalists.

hints: What does Wells do with her evidence?
candidates.remember: A purpose answer should cover the whole text.

candidates.subskill: Finite verb in a main clause
candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: Octavia E. Butler, whose novels include
candidates.explanation: The subject "Octavia E. Butler" needs a finite verb; the clause after it is set off by commas, and "became" fits the past event.

A.rationale: "Becoming" is not a finite verb, so the sentence would lack a main verb.

C.rationale: "Having become" is not a finite verb, so the sentence would lack a main verb.

D.rationale: "To become" is not a finite verb, so the sentence would lack a main verb.

hints: Does the sentence have a main verb?

strategy.explanation: Skip the clause between the commas.

candidates.remember: Every sentence needs a finite main verb.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: The passengers belonged to one elevator, the one Dunbar operated, so the singular possessive "elevator's" is correct.

B.rationale: The plural possessive refers to more than one elevator, but Dunbar operated one.

C.rationale: A plural noun without an apostrophe cannot show possession here.

D.rationale: "Elevators's" is not a correct possessive form.

strategy.explanation: Decide singular or plural, then possessive.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.explanation: The city was abandoned, yet people continued to know and live on it, so a concessive transition fits.

A.rationale: The city's abandonment did not cause it to be remembered.

B.rationale: The farmers' presence is not an example of the abandonment.

C.rationale: Being remembered is not similar to being abandoned.

hints: Does the second sentence agree with or qualify the first?
candidates.remember: Use a concessive transition when a fact qualifies the one before it.

candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize that Anning's contributions were not fully credited during her lifetime. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Mary Anning, who collected fossils near Lyme Regis, is now recognized as an important early paleontologist.
choices.B: In 1823, Mary Anning found the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaur, a marine reptile.
choices.C: Although Anning found the first complete plesiosaur, scientists often published her fossils without naming her.
choices.D: Mary Anning collected fossils on the cliffs near Lyme Regis, England, from 1799 to 1847.

candidates.evidence: Scientists often bought her fossils and described them in publications without naming her
candidates.explanation: Only choice C pairs her major find with the fact that scientists published her fossils without crediting her.

A.rationale: This emphasizes her present recognition, not the lack of credit in her lifetime.

B.rationale: This states her achievement but not the lack of credit.

D.rationale: This gives background, and she was not collecting from birth.

hints: Which note shows a lack of credit?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against the goal.

candidates.remember: A synthesis answer must address the stated goal.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the student's claim?

choices.A: Germination rose from 40% with no soaking to 62% after 6 hours of soaking.
choices.B: Germination was 78% after 12 hours of soaking and 77% after 24 hours.
choices.C: Germination after 12 hours of soaking was 16 percentage points higher than after 6 hours.
choices.D: Every soaking time produced higher germination than no soaking.

candidates.evidence: soaking longer than 12 hours provided no additional benefit
candidates.explanation: Comparing 12 hours (78%) with 24 hours (77%) shows that longer soaking added nothing.

A.rationale: This shows a benefit of short soaking, not the lack of benefit after 12 hours.

C.rationale: This shows a benefit from soaking up to 12 hours, not the lack of benefit beyond 12 hours.

D.rationale: This is true but does not address soaking beyond 12 hours.

hints: Which two values test the claim?

strategy.explanation: Find the data on both sides of 12 hours.

candidates.remember: Support a claim with the data it is about.

revision_history.reason: blind solver: distractor "highest, 78%, after 12 hours" implied the 24-hour comparison and partly supported the claim

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would Hawkins (Text 2) most likely respond to Reiche's argument in Text 1?

choices.A: He would agree that the lines were a calendar but say they tracked only the Sun.
choices.B: He would argue that the lines were created much later than Reiche believed.
choices.C: He would claim that the lines were definitely paths connected to water.
choices.D: He would say the evidence does not show that the lines were aimed at the sky.

candidates.evidence: no more often than lines pointing in random directions would
candidates.explanation: Hawkins tested the calendar idea and found the alignments were no more frequent than chance, which undercuts Reiche's argument.

A.rationale: Hawkins found no meaningful alignment with any astronomical events.

B.rationale: Text 2 says nothing about when the lines were made.

C.rationale: Text 2 attributes the ritual-path idea to later researchers and calls the water link possible.

strategy.explanation: Compare Hawkins's finding with Reiche's claim.

candidates.remember: Identify whether a second text supports or undermines the first.

revision_history.reason: both solvers: key copied Text 2 nearly verbatim and "such events" had no referent
